newsitem.title: GERMANY: MGAM woes prompt German watchdog to survey funds.
newsitem.headline: MGAM woes prompt German watchdog to survey funds.

text.p: Germany's bank watchdog, reacting to suspected irregularities at London-based Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), has asked fund managers in Germany to reveal their holdings of unlisted shares, fund group DWS said on Monday.
A spokesman for DWS, which like MGAM is a subsidiary of Deutsche Bank AG, said DWS had "minimal" holdings of unlisted companies or companies that were about to be listed.
Under European Union-wide regulations, investment funds are not allowed to invest more than 10 percent of their money in unlisted securities.
"It varies from three percent to 0.5 percent to nil, depending on the fund," the DWS spokesman said in response to a Reuter enquiry. "There is no case in which we hit the 10 percent level."
German daily Boersen-Zeitung said the Federal Banking Supervisory Authority had asked about a dozen domestic fund managers to provide information.

Investors last week dumped units in three of MGAM's unit trusts following news that the trusts had breached regulations by investing more that 10 percent of their funds in speculative, unlisted, high-technology European stocks.
The manager of two of the funds, Peter Young, has been suspended and his personal assets frozen pending a probe into the management of funds.
The news rattled investor confidence in unit trusts, seen hitherto as a safe place to put one's money.

The German Banking Supervisory Office would neither confirm or deny that it had asked German fund managers for up-to-date information. The Office reviews compliance at investment companies annually by reviewing auditors' reports.
A spokesman for the watchdog said, "In the past, the maximum permitted level of such holdings has not been reached."

A spokesman for Deutscher Investment Trust (DIT), the fund unit of Dresdner Bank AG could neither confirm nor deny whether it had been asked to give information but said its investments in unlisted securities were "virtually nil."
